Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) 2 NIST Policy on the Use of the SI In accordance with various Federal Acts, the Code of Federal Regulations, and Executive Order 12770 (see Preface), it is NIST policy that the SI shall be used in all NIST publications. 1 When the field of application or the special needs of users of NIST publications require the use of other units, the values of quantities shall first be expressed in acceptable units, where it is to be understood that acceptable units include the SI units and those units recognized for use with the SI; the corresponding values expressed in the other units shall then follow in parentheses. (For precise definitions of the terms “SI units” and “acceptable units” as used in this Guide, see Sec. 5.4.) Exceptions to this policy require the prior approval of the NIST Director. The following three sections—2.1 Essential data, 2.1.1 Tables and graphs, and 2.2 Descriptive information—elaborate upon this policy. 2.1 Essential data Essential data express or interpret quantitative results. All such data shall be given in acceptable units. In those cases where — the sole use of acceptable units would compromise good communication,

2.2 Descriptive information—elaborate upon this policy. 2.1 Essential data Essential data express or interpret quantitative results. All such data shall be given in acceptable units. In those cases where — the sole use of acceptable units would compromise good communication, or — units other than acceptable units have been specified as a contractual requirement, values of quantities shall be given in acceptable units followed, in parentheses, by the values of the same quantities given in the other units. Exceptions may sometimes be necessary for commercial devices, technical standards, or quantities having special legal significance; examples include commercial weights and measures devices and the related laws and regulations. However, even in such cases, values of quantities expressed in acceptable units should be used when possible with the same values expressed in other units following in parentheses. 2.1.1 Tables and graphs In tables, values of quantities expressed in acceptable units and the corresponding values expressed in other units may be shown in parallel columns, with the acceptable-unit column preceding the other-unit column. In graphs, axes labeled in other units shall be given secondary status. This may preferably be done by placing scale marks on and labeling the left-hand ordinate and bottom abscissa

parallel columns, with the acceptable-unit column preceding the other-unit column. In graphs, axes labeled in other units shall be given secondary status. This may preferably be done by placing scale marks on and labeling the left-hand ordinate and bottom abscissa in acceptable units, and placing scale marks on and labeling the right-hand ordinate and top abscissa in other units. Alternatively, lighter-weight scale marks and smaller type may be employed to indicate other units using the same ordinate and abscissa as is used for the acceptable units. 2.2 Descriptive information Descriptive information characterizes arrangements, environments, the generalized dimensions of objects, apparatus, or materials, and other attributes that do not enter directly into calculations or results. When necessary for effective communication, such information may be expressed using customary terms that are widely used and recognized. Examples include common drill sizes and traditional tools used in the United States, U.S. standard fastener sizes, commercial pipe sizes, and other common terms used in the trades, the professions, the marketplace, sports, and various social activities. The local force of gravity on a body, that is, its weight, consists of the resultant of all the gravitational forces acting on the body and the local centrifugal force due to the rotation of the celestial object. The effect of atmospheric buoyancy is usually excluded, and thus the weight of a body is generally the local force of gravity on the body in vacuum. In commercial and everyday use, and especially in common parlance, weight is usually used as a synonym for mass. Thus the SI unit of the quantity weight used in this sense is the kilogram (kg) and the verb “to weigh” means “to determine the mass of” or “to have a mass of.” Examples: the child’s weight is 23 kg the briefcase weighs 6 kg 23 Net wt. 227 g

In any case, in order to avoid confusion, whenever the word “weight” is used, it should be made clear which meaning is intended. 8.4 Relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass The terms atomic weight and molecular weight are obsolete and thus should be avoided. They have been replaced by the equivalent but preferred terms relative atomic mass, symbol Ar, and relative molecular mass, symbol Mr, respectively [4: ISO 31-8], which better reflect their definitions. Similar to atomic weight and molecular weight, relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass are quantities of dimension one and are expressed simply as numbers. The definitions of these quantities are as follows [4: ISO 31-8]: Relative atomic mass (formerly atomic weight): ratio of the average mass per atom of an element to 1/12 of the mass of the atom of the nuclide 12C. Relative molecular mass (formerly molecular weight): ratio of the average mass per molecule or

In publications dealing with mass spectrometry, one often encounters statements such as “the mass-to-charge ratio is 15.” What is usually meant in this case is that the ratio of the nucleon number (that is, mass number—see Sec. 10.4.2) of the ion to its number of charges is 15. Thus mass-to-charge ratio is a quantity of dimension one, even though it is commonly denoted by the symbol m / z. For example, the mass-to-charge ratio of the ion 12C71H7+ + is 91/2 = 45.5. 8.5 Temperature interval and temperature difference As discussed in Sec. 4.2.1.1, Celsius temperature (t) is defined in terms of thermodynamic temperature (T) by the equation t = T − T0, where T0 = 273.15 K by definition. Definition: mass of substance B divided by the mass of the mixture: wB = mB / m. 8.7 Logarithmic quantities and units: level, neper, bel This section briefly introduces logarithmic quantities and units. It is based on Ref. [5: IEC 60027-3], which should be consulted for further details. Two of the most common logarithmic quantities are level-ofa-field-quantity, symbol LF, and level-of-a-power-quantity, symbol LP; and two of the most common logarithmic units are the units in which the values of these quantities are expressed: the neper, symbol Np, or the bel, symbol B, and decimal multiples and submultiples of the neper and bel formed by attaching SI 28

Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) prefixes to them, such as the millineper, symbol mNp (1 mNp = 0.001 Np), and the decibel, symbol dB (1 dB = 0.1 B). Level-of-a-field-quantity is defined by the relation LF = ln(F/F0), where F/F0 is the ratio of two amplitudes of the same kind, F0 being a reference amplitude. Level-of-a-power-quantity is defined by the relation LP = (1/2) ln(P/P0), where P/P0 is the ratio of two powers, P0 being a reference power. (Note that if P/P0 = (F/F0)2, then LP = LF.) Similar names, symbols, and definitions apply to levels based on other quantities which are linear or quadratic functions of the amplitudes, respectively. In practice, the name of the field quantity forms the name of LF and the symbol F is replaced by the symbol of the field quantity. For example, if the field quantity in question is electric field strength, symbol E, the name of the quantity is “level-of-electric-field-strength” and it is defined by the relation LE = ln(E/E0). The difference between two levels-of-a-field-quantity (called “field-level difference”) having the same reference amplitude F0 is ΔLF = LF1 − LF2 = ln(F1/F0) − ln(F2/F0) = ln(F1/F2), and

quantity is “level-of-electric-field-strength” and it is defined by the relation LE = ln(E/E0). rules and style conventions related to spelling the names of units. 9.1 Capitalization When spelled out in full, unit names are treated like ordinary English nouns. Thus the names of all units start with a lower-case letter, except at the beginning of a sentence or in capitalized material such as a title. In keeping with this rule, the correct spelling of the name of the unit ºC is “degree Celsius” (the unit “degree” begins with a lowercase “d” and the modifier “Celsius” begins with an uppercase “C” because it is the name of a person). 9.2 Plurals Plural unit names are used when they are required by the rules of English grammar. They are normally formed regularly, for example, “henries” is the plural of henry. According to Ref. [6], the following plurals are irregular: Singular —lux, hertz, siemens; Plural —lux, hertz, siemens. (See also Sec. 9.7.) 9.3 Spelling unit names with prefixes When the name of a unit containing a prefix is spelled out, no space or hyphen is used between the prefix and unit name (see Sec. 6.2.3). Examples: milligram but not: milli-gram kilopascal but not: kilo-pascal Reference [6] points out that there are three cases in which the

prefix is spelled out, no space or hyphen is used between the prefix and unit name (see Sec. 6.2.3). Examples: milligram but not: milli-gram kilopascal but not: kilo-pascal Reference [6] points out that there are three cases in which the final vowel of an SI prefix is commonly omitted: megohm (not megaohm), kilohm (not kiloohm), and hectare (not hectoare). In all other cases in which the unit name begins with a vowel, both the final vowel of the prefix and the vowel of the unit name are retained and both are pronounced. 9.4 Spelling unit names obtained by multiplication When the name of a derived unit formed from other units by multiplication is spelled out, a space, which is preferred by Ref. [6] and this Guide, or a hyphen is used to separate the names of the individual units. 31

Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) Example: 9.5 pascal second or pascal-second Spelling unit names obtained by division When the name of a derived unit formed from other units by division is spelled out, the word “per” is used and not a solidus. (See also Secs. 6.1.7 and 9.8.) Example: 9.6 ampere per meter (A/m) but not: ampere/meter Spelling unit names raised to powers When the names of units raised to powers are spelled out, modifiers such as “squared” or “cubed” are used and are placed after the unit name. Example: meter per second squared (m/s2) The modifiers “square” or “cubic” may, however, be placed before the unit name in the case of area or volume. Examples: 9.7 square centimeter (cm2) cubic millimeter (mm3) ampere per square meter (A/m2) kilogram per cubic meter (kg/m3) Other spelling conventions A derived unit is usually singular in English, for example, the value 3 m2·K/W is usually spelled out as “three square meter kelvin per watt,” and the value 3 C·m2/V is usually spelled out as “three coulomb meter squared per volt.” However, a “single” unit may be plural; for example, the value 5 kPa is spelled out as

as “three square meter kelvin per watt,” and the value 3 C·m2/V is usually spelled out as “three coulomb meter squared per volt.” However, a “single” unit may be plural; for example, the value 5 kPa is spelled out as “five kilopascals,” although “five kilopascal” is acceptable. If in such a single-unit case the number is less than one, the unit is always singular when spelled out; for example, 0.5 kPa is spelled out as “fivetenths kilopascal.” Note: 9.8 These other spelling conventions are given for completeness; as indicated in Sec. 7.6, it is the position of this Guide that symbols for numbers and units should be used to express the values of quantities, not the spelled-out names of numbers and units. Reference [3] also requires that a symbol for a number be used whenever the value of a quantity is expressed in terms of a unit of measurement. Unacceptability of applying mathematical operations to unit names Because it could possibly lead to confusion, mathematical operations are not applied to unit names but only to unit symbols. Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) 10.1 Kinds of symbols Letter symbols are of three principal kinds: (a) symbols for quantities, (b) symbols for units, and (c) symbols for descriptive terms. Quantity symbols, which are always printed in italic (that is, sloping) type, are, with few exceptions, single letters of the Latin or Greek alphabets that may have subscripts or superscripts or other identifying signs. Symbols for units, in particular those for acceptable units, have been discussed in detail in earlier portions of this Guide. B.5 Factor for converting motor vehicle efficiency The efficiency of motor vehicles in the United States is commonly expressed in miles per U.S. gallon, while in most other countries it is expressed in liters per one hundred kilometers. To convert fuel economy stated in miles per U.S. gallon to fuel consumption expressed in L/(100 km), divide 235.215 by the numerical value of the stated fuel economy. Examples: 6.974 951 5 rounded to 7 digits is 6.974 952 6.974 950 5 rounded to 7 digits is 6.974 950 B.7.2 Rounding converted numerical values of quantities The use of the factors given in Secs. B.8 and B.9 to convert values of quantities was demonstrated in Sec. B.3. In most cases the product of the unconverted numerical value and the factor will be a numerical value with a number of digits that exceeds the number of significant digits (see Sec. 7.9) of the unconverted numerical value. Proper conversion procedure requires rounding this converted numerical value to the number of significant digits that is consistent with the maximum possible rounding error of the unconverted numerical value. Example: To express the value l = 36 ft in meters, use the factor 3.048 E−01 from Sec. B.8 or Sec. B.9 and write l = 36 ft × 0.3048 m/ft = 10.9728 m = 11.0 m. 43

Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) The final result, l = 11.0 m, is based on the following reasoning: The numerical value “36” has two significant digits, and thus a relative maximum possible rounding error (abbreviated RE in this Guide for simplicity) of ± 0.5/36 = ± 1.4 %, because it could have resulted from rounding the number 35.5, 36.5, or any number between 35.5 and 36.5. To be consistent with this RE, the converted numerical value “10.9728” is rounded to 11.0 or three significant digits because the number 11.0 has an RE of ± 0.05/11.0 = ± 0.45 %. Although this ± 0.45 % RE is one-third of the ± 1.4 % RE of the unconverted numerical value “36,” if the converted numerical value “10.9728” had been rounded to 11 or two significant digits, information contained in the unconverted numerical value “36” would have been lost. This is because the RE of the numerical value “11” is ± 0.5/11 = ± 4.5 %, which is three times the ± 1.4 % RE of the unconverted numerical value “36.” This example therefore shows that when selecting the number of digits to retain in the numerical

value “11” is ± 0.5/11 = ± 4.5 %, which is three times the ± 1.4 % RE of the unconverted numerical value “36.” This example therefore shows that when selecting the number of digits to retain in the numerical value of a converted quantity, one must often choose between discarding information or providing unwarranted information. Consideration of the end use of the converted value can often help one decide which choice to make. Note: Consider that one had been told initially that the value l = 36 ft had been rounded to the nearest inch. Then in this case, since l is known to within ± 1 in, the RE of the numerical value “36” is ± 1 in/(36 ft × 12 in/ft) = ± 0.23 %. Although this is less than the ± 0.45 % RE of the number 11.0, it is comparable to it. Therefore, the result l = 11.0 m is still given as the converted value. (Note that the numerical value “10.97” would give excessive unwarranted information because it has an RE that is one-fifth of ± 0.23 %.) 44

SI COHERENT DERIVED UNITS WITH SPECIAL NAMES AND SYMBOLS (Explanation of Graphic on Back Cover) Derived units are defined as products of powers of the base units. When the product of powers includes no numerical factor other than one, the derived units are called “coherent derived” units. The base and coherent derived units of the SI form a coherent set, designated the set of “coherent SI units.” The word coherent is used here in the following sense: when coherent units are used, equations between the numerical values of quantities take exactly the same form as the equations between the quantities themselves. Thus, if only units from a coherent set are used, conversion factors between units are never required. The diagram on the back page of SP811 shows graphically how the 22 SI coherent derived units with special names and symbols are related to the seven SI base units. 1. In the first column, the symbols of the SI base units are shown in rectangles, with the name of the unit shown toward the upper left of the rectangle and the name of the associated base quantity shown in italic type below the rectangle. 2. of European chemists. Recently, however, some very careful analyses of American mushrooms have been made. The results of these investigations, while in general accord with the work already done in Europe, have emphasized the fact that mushrooms are of very variable composition. That different species should vary greatly was of course to be expected, but we now know that different specimens of the same species grown under different conditions may be markedly different in chemical composition. The chief factors causing this variation are the composition, the moisture content, and the temperature of the soil in which they grow, together with the maturity of the plant. The temperature, humidity, and movement of the atmosphere and other local conditions have a further influence on the amount of water present. The process of drying mushrooms for winter use is most extensive practice by the peasantry of Europe and Britain, who thus find an all-the-year- round dein pendence upon mushroom diet. With most species this process of desiccation is so simple that it is recommended, in the confident belief that, once tried, the winter mushroom will hereafter afford a frequent relish upon many a board and will well repay the slight trouble in their summer preparation. In most of the Agarics notably the Campestris, Procerus, Champignon, Russula, Chantarelle simply threading on strings and hanging in the sun and wind, or festooned above the kitchen range, will be sufficient to reduce them to complete dryness in a few hours. Indeed, some of these, such as the Procerus and Champignon, dry spontaneously in their haunts, and may be thus gathered. PREFACE In response to the very numerous inquiries received during past years from interested students and correspondents, this account of common edible and poisonous fungi of Canada has been prepared. While no attempt has been made to deal with all the higher fungi of Canada, few, if any, have been omitted that should be included among the commonest to be found throughout the Dominion. The bulletin is not intended as a ‘‘learned treatise,’’ but is meant to appeal to students as well as nature lovers, who wish to know the many odd or beautiful forms of fungous growth they may happen upon in their country rambles. In consequence, an arrangement has been followed not of a strictly scientific nature, but of a more or less alphabetical grouping, especially of the species mentioned herein. My best thanks are due to my friend and collaborator, Mr. W. S. Odell, whose practical experience, together with the vast amount of material collected by him, has alone made this publication possible. The excellent photographs were taken—unless otherwise indicated—by G. G. Clarke, Chief of the Photographic Division of the Geological Survey, from specimens collected by Mr. Odell on his frequent jaunts through woods and meadows. For

GIEALLE THE NATURE, GENERAL Rel STRUCTURE, CLASSIFICATION DEVELOPMENT, AND OF FUNGI The more elaborately “‘living things” are organized, the higher is the place they hold in any system of classification. Accordingly, man is regarded as the highest type of animal. The lower animals possess no specialized, intricate organization, and thus are popularly referred to as of low or lower rank. In the vegetable kingdom the same distinction rules. Thus we have higher plants—essentially so the flowering plants—in which the organs are more complex than in those groups possessing no flowers, correspondingly known as lower plants. The term “fungus” (plural ‘‘fungi’’) designates a particular group of non-flowering plants, closely related to algae and lichens. Seaweeds of all types are algae. “Reindeer moss” is not a moss but a common species of the group of lichens. These plants differ from other non-flowering plants of a higher order, such as the ferns, in having no vascular system, i.e., an arrangement of - spiral and similar vessels so prominent when the stem of a rhubarb leaf is torn in two. Furthermore, fungi contain no chlorophyll, which substance is responsible in other plants for their green colour. The term includes all species dealt with in

and similar vessels so prominent when the stem of a rhubarb leaf is torn in two. Furthermore, fungi contain no chlorophyll, which substance is responsible in other plants for their green colour. The term includes all species dealt with in these pages, edible or poisonous. Toadstools, popularly looked upon as poisonous, are fungi just the same as any other kind, though referred to under this name with the intention of distinguishing them from the edible kinds, popularly known as mushrooms. Unfortunately, the terms have no significance in distinguishing the good from the bad, the edible from the poisonous, even though this distinction is exceedingly common. Owing to the lack of chlorophyll (which substance, aside from giving the green colour to plants, assists materially in the manufacture of plant food), fungi, generally speaking, depend for their growth and development upon food materials manufactured by the living plant. Thus dependent, their mode of life is that of a parasite, like the rusts, smuts, and other fungi; or they may find their food requirements in dead organic matter, when their mode of life is termed “saprophytic.” Fungi do not produce roots as do higher plants, nor flowers, nor seeds. GENERAL STRUCTURE OF FUNGI : UG The true reproductive organs of a fungus are known as “spores” (Pl. 4 **). Inasmuch as spores are able to germinate (PI. 4'°), they are often likened to seeds, but a true seed is much more highly organized, containing the well-defined embryo or young plant, surrounded or furnished with a supply of food for the use of this young plant when it develops (Pl. 4°). Fungi differ materially in size and structure; they may be microscopic or very minute in size, or they may present themselves as very formidable objects. Thus our collection at Ottawa contains some woody or bracket fungi (Ganoderma applanatum) twelve by twenty-four inches in size, as well as at least one giant puffball more than three times the size of a football. In structure the smallest forms are most wonderful, beautiful, and interesting objects for microscopical study; and their organization, structure, and precise functions bear remarkable testimony to the Creator’s wondrous skill. Their variations in colour alone defy all attempts at classifying them or describing the marvellous tints that may be met with. For this purpose it is desirable to briefly review the life-history of a fungus, that is to say, to observe all phases and changes that occur from the commencement of the germinating spore to the production of a new generationof spores. It would be a difficult task in a popular account, and altogether too complicated, to deal with the many deviations that occur in individual genera from the simple developments here Cescribed. The mature spore of a mushroom, finding conditions suitable for growth, absorbs moisture and increases in size. Eventually its cell wall or covering membrane ruptures or is pierced from within by the germ tube—the first sign of germination—which later branches and continues to branch freely until the substratum or matter upon which it grows is permeated in all directions by a dense network of hyphae, collectively referred to as ‘“‘mycelium.’’ This mycelium absorbs nutriments, and thus functions similarly to the root-system of flowering plants. The production of spores in nature from a single mushroom amounts to millions. On germination of so

dense network of hyphae, collectively referred to as ‘“‘mycelium.’’ This mycelium absorbs nutriments, and thus functions similarly to the root-system of flowering plants. The production of spores in nature from a single mushroom amounts to millions. On germination of so many spores within a small space, the mycelia of these spores frequently unite by fusion, eventually giving rise to one or more fruiting bodies. At first there become visible to the naked eye dense masses of hyphae, forming gradually into small nodules, increasing until they resemble a pea in size and shape, and finally growing into the so-called “button” stage, so often referred to in the literature dealing with the development of mushrooms. The button expands, and the perfect fungus results (Pl. 14), which soon teems with a new generation of spores, to continue its life-cycle as described. |

GENERAL STRUCTURE, BASIDIOMYCETES 17 The perfect fungus is really a fruiting body varying in shape and structure, carrying the spores in some manner or other; hence technically spoken of as a ‘‘sporophore.”” On frequent occasions the immediate surroundings of a mature sporophore will be found covered with a dense deposit of fungus spores, covering the ground, leaves, blades of grasses, etc., with a fine white or variously coloured dust. The mechanism of spore dispersal and the methods of their general dissemination in nature are most interesting phases to observe, and those interested in a closer study of these remarkable plants are referred to our list of suitable works from which they may gather additional and more precise information. t The manner or mode of production of spores is, broadly speaking, used as a fundamental basis for the classification of fungi. Among the larger fungi, to which the pages of this account are confined, we may observe two fundamental methods of spore production, which affordsan opportunity of establishing two main groups. In the first, the spores—usually four in number—are produced by special cells, forming a dense layer, the fruiting layer, or, technically, hymenium (Pl. 4). Individually » the spore-bearing cell is

In the first, the spores—usually four in number—are produced by special cells, forming a dense layer, the fruiting layer, or, technically, hymenium (Pl. 4). Individually » the spore-bearing cell is known as ‘‘basidium”’ (plural “‘basidia’’). All basidia are microscopic in size and cannot be seen with the naked eye. We refer our readers, in order to familiarize them with their appearance, to plate 4" of our explanatory sketches. Usually they are more or less club-shaped, colourless cells, bearing a number of fine, delicate points at the apex; corresponding to the number of spores produced at the tips. These spores are known as “‘basidio spores,” being borne by a basidium. From this characteristic, this first group of fungi is known as “BASIDIOMYCETES”’ or ‘‘Basidio-fungi.”’ The second main group exhibits an entirely different method of spore production. Here the spores, however produced, are without exception contained singly or in odd or even numbers, usually eight, in special spore cases or sacs (Pl. 48). Technically this sac is known as an “‘ascus’’; hence this group has received the designation of ‘“AscomycETEs” or ‘‘Asco-fungi.”’ XN FIRST MAIN GROUP BASIDIOMYCETES In this large main group

20 MUSHROOMS AND TOADSTOOLS First Division GILL FUNGI Before studying, however, any other characters of the species in this group, we must determine the spore colour of any specimen under observation. The colour of the gills themselves is no indication of the colour of the spores borne by them. Neither is the colour of the spores viewed under the microscope of much significance. Similarly, a drop of blood examined under the microscope will not appear blood-red in colour. What is meant by the determination of the spore colour is the colour of the spores en masse. There is a very easy and fascinating method, viz. the making of a spore print. For this purpose, cut away the cap from the stem immediately below the gills. The more perfect the specimen selected, and the more care taken, the more beautiful and com- plete will be the resulting spore print. Of course, even a small portion of the cap will yield a print satisfactory enough for the determination of the spore colour. If doubtful as to the colour of spores, make a print on both kinds of paper. This is especially recommended when one specimen only is available. Cover the cap with a tumbler or bell-jar, and allow to remain undisturbed for a time, when a beautifully shaped deposit will appear on the paper (PI. 3°), corresponding to the arrangement of the gills and showing unmistakably the colour of the spore mass. By means of the most wonderful natural principles of engineering, these spores are discharged one or thousands at a time without touching or interfering with each other. GENERAL STRUCTURE, GILL FUNGI 21 To begin with, the cap varies in colour, yet the colour may vary so considerably within a species, according to age and condition or place of growth, that it does not always afford conclusive proof of its identity. The cap may show other characters which should be carefully observed. If centrally deeply depressed like a funnel, it is termed “funnel- shaped”’ (infundibulate) (Pls. 4¥; 22”); when slightly depressed in the centre it is umbilicate (PI. 52); or umbonate when erally elevated (Pls. 4"; 12); convex when curved downwards; concave when the Margin turns upward in a saucer-like fashion; plane when even and straight. The margin of the cap may be thin or thick, hairy or bearing appendages; it may be reflexed or turned up; involute or rolled up inward; repand, when wavy; striate when marked with lines corresponding to the gills below. The upper surface of the cap may be smooth, velvety, shiny, dry, sticky, glued, or covered with tufts or scales, or marked with concentric rings, etc., etc. The gills also show remarkable variation. -Their own colour is fairly constant, and certainly does not vary within the species nearly as much as the colour

glued, or covered with tufts or scales, or marked with concentric rings, etc., etc. The gills also show remarkable variation. -Their own colour is fairly constant, and certainly does not vary within the species nearly as much as the colour of the cap.. They, therefore, constitute a valuable aid to identification. But it is principally the relation of the gills to the stem which must be observed, since this feature, being very constant, affords additional help in determining a fungus of the gill-bearing type. The gills may thus be quite free from, or may be squarely joined to the stem (adnate); or they may only partly join the stem (adnexed); they may continue down the stem for a distance (decurrent); they may be notched; wavy, waxy, forked, etc., etc. (Pl. 4"). The remainder are corky, woody, soft at first and hardening with age, or dry, leathery, though often remarkably beautifully marked and coloured. The commonest forms of this group are globular, flask or pear-shaped, solid, fleshy balls of various sizes and dimensions, popularly known as “puffballs.” The solid, fleshy interior gradually changes into a spore-filled, dry ball, correctly termed puffball, because at the least touch “‘pufts’’ of spores will be discharged either through a round or lacerated hole at the apex or through fissures and ruptures of the covering walls. In several genera the outer walls break into segments, which open out and form a star-shape on the ground. These are popularly known as “earth stars.’ The common “‘bird-nest’”’ fungi also form a division of this group.

GHABTER HINTS IV TO COLLECTORS The facility and ease with which a correct determination of a fungus may be made, depends largely upon the more or less perfect and normal condition of the specimen. Dry seasons and the heat of the sun generally, produce peculiar changes; the distinctive characters present during ordinarily humid conditions are thus often changed beyond recognition; excessively wet weather also results in emphasizing certain features upon which no great stress should ordinarily be laid. After spells of dry weather the surface of the cap may show reticulations not present in normal’ forms. Spells of rain may affect the general appearance as well as the colour and condition of the cap. Light and shade, or mechanical interferences may cause twisting and curving of stems, not normal. For these and other reasons a beginner may encounter serious difficulties in’ correctly determining a species. Only when large numbers of specimens have been studied, preferably under all conditions of growth, will it become more easy to properly regard the curious changes brought about by such influences. In species growing in clumps there occur variations in shape due to the pressure of one member of a group against another, but this

will it become more easy to properly regard the curious changes brought about by such influences. In species growing in clumps there occur variations in shape due to the pressure of one member of a group against another, but this cause will be ever remembered when once observed on the occasion of a collecting trip. It is more difficult when abnormal specimens are submitted for identification without any notes or comments. Under such circumstances it is well to remember what has been said above. First of all, it is wise to become familiar with the normal forms, to which these pages are devoted. In collecting fungi an open eye should be kept when roaming through fields and meadows, woods and mountain sides, for old stumps, the harbourer often of prolific and instructive associations, or for ‘‘fairy rings,”’ a circular growth formation frequently assumed by some of our native fungi. Dump-heaps, piles of decaying sawdust or mill refuse, manure piles, lawns, and meadows, especially where animals have grazed, should be carefully surveyed. Fungi once located in goodly numbers in such spots may yield many a good harvest on future occasions. No special outfit is needed in collecting mushrooms; an ordinary fruit

and meadows, especially where animals have grazed, should be carefully surveyed. Fungi once located in goodly numbers in such spots may yield many a good harvest on future occasions. No special outfit is needed in collecting mushrooms; an ordinary fruit basket, a strong knife or pointed stick, twine, strong paper to cover the basket, tissue paper as used in wrapping apples or oranges, and waxed paper for the more sticky forms, is all that is required. Cardboard boxes to protect small and fragile specimens will come in very useful. Grass, leaves, or moss packed loosely but firmly around each plant as collected, will protect them from damage and injury, thereby preserving many a dainty character that would otherwise be lost. Most of the specimens of fleshy fungi sent in for identification, reach us in a putrid and decayed condition, rendering determination often impossible. Such conditions can be avoided to some extent by care in packing, but above all, by the selection of sound specimens. Once invaded by maggots—and few are not—it is merely a question of hours before they will have changed into an unsavoury mess. 29

The species of this genus should present no serious difficulties in identifying, because of several prominent and important characters distinguishing them from other fungi. The conspicuous egg-shape of the young plant, entirely covered by a thick volva, the prominent curtain or veil-like ring, and the typical cup at the base of the stem of the mature plant, are features which emphatically impress the student. The cap is fleshy, at first convex, becoming expanded. The gills are free from the stem, which is central and different in substance from the cap, and is readily separated from it. _The genus is small, but highly interesting on account of the character and bright colouring of the cap in certain species. 62 MUSHROOMS AND TOADSTOOLS This is a truly remarkable and interesting plant. Once its large clumps have been found— conspicuous in daytime by their bright saffron-yellow colour, and wonderful to behold on dark On what grounds the author called this beautiful plant ‘“‘illudens” (deceiving), we cannot comprehend. Perchance because, notwithstanding its innocent beauty, it is disappointing in taste and often seriously injurious when eaten. The phenomenon of luminescence so wonderfully shown by this fungus occurs in many other forms of fungi (Armillaria, Panus, etc.), and is no doubt responsible for much of the superstitions attached to fungi-generally. It is a natural phenomenon, and may be observed any dark night or in a darkened room once the eye is accustomed to the darkness. The intensity of the light given off by these fungi varies often according to age and condition. It is generally bright enough to affect sensitive photographic plates. CAP Almost throughout brittle plants, readily distinguished from fungi of similar size, shape, and colour by the exudation of a milky, cloudy juice, which oozes freely from any broken or damaged portion. This juice is generally white, but in some species changes in colour on exposure to air, becoming yellow, red, or violet. The gills are particularly milky. The taste of the milk frequently aids in distinguishing species, and should be noted. It may be mild at first, then peppery and acrid, which taste may persist in one’s mouth for some time. Russula, a genus resembling Lactarius rather closely, never shows the characteristic fluid, even though occasionally a trace of a clear, serous fluid may be observed in the former. For with knowledge and care, fatalities due to the eating of poisonous kinds may be wholly avoided. Our first recommendation, therefore, would be: Eat no fungus of any kind unknown to you. Assume not the slightest risk, and make sure that all specimens collected are safe to eat. It is a thorough knowledge only, that constitutes the greatest measure of safety. At present this knowledge is fundamentally lacking; and it is something of a surprise that fatalities are not more frequent. We have on occasions observed people collecting all kinds of fungi, who assured In us they were all safe to eat, and yet had no knowledge by which to identify any of them. consequence of lack of knowledge, there are spoiling every year in Canada, many hundreds of varieties of edible fungi, that might form a most welcome change in one’s diet. We would further suggest that all mixtures of fungi—the result of haphazard collection—should be avoided. Too often a poisonous kind might be found in such collections. They are most valuable as savouries, flavours, and condiments. Generally speaking, all substances consumed for the nourishment of the body may be regarded as food. Chemical analysis has divided food substances into two fundamental groups, viz. nitrogenous (proteins and nitrogenous extracts), and non-nitrogenous (carbohydrates, fats, etc., etc.). Raw beef contains about 20 per cent nitrogenous substances; fresh vegetables about 3 to 4 per cent; fresh table mushrooms from 7 to 8 per cent, the chanterelle about 3 to 4 per cent, the oyster fungus 3 to 4 per cent, the morel about 7 to 8 per cent, and so on. Of non-nitrogenous substances there exist in fungi about 4 per cent, in vegetables about 3 ‘per cent, while in meat there are practically none. Fungi are composed of a high percentage of water—93 to 95 per cent as compared to lean beef with 70 per cent and fresh vegetables with about 92 per cent. Fungi also contain small amounts of nutritive salts and sugar. Further researches may reveal the presence of useful vitamines;

Let all fungi, especially, be fresh, and do not use them at all if ever so slightly touched by decay. Avoid old, maggoty, and water-soaked specimens. This fear is due, we repeat, most frequently to lack of knowledge; and it is hoped that this account may serve to educate people to a different and more correct frame of mind toward s fungi. The subject might with advantage be introdu ced into the curricula of our schools, since a knowledge of the means of distinguishing the poisonous from the edible fungi is just as import ant as a knowledge of poisonous plants generally. There exist several treatises on poison ous plants occurring in Canada, but so far no exhaustive one is available on poisonous fungi. We shall always be pleased to answer any inquirie s in regard to fungi, and would indeed appreciate contributions from any locality of Canada in order to complete our knowledge of the kind and frequency of these plants in other districts. The term “spawn” has become familiar to our readers. The spawn is taken from vigorously growing beds or from artificial cultures of the varieties of the common mushroom usually grown. Its presence is often revealed by a most offensive odour, and on hunting for the cause of this, there will be found, especially among the younger stages, decaying and often malformed “buttons” and young mushrooms that have turned into a putrid mass. Immediately such specimens have been discovered they should be removed very carefully, and no sound specimen should be touched by hand or implement when removing diseased ones. These should be placed in a paper bag and burned at once. Wherever removed from the bed it is suggested that a handful of unslaked lime be scattered over the surface of the affected patch and its immediate surrounding. A careful daily examination, repeating this treatment when new specimens are found affected, is absolutely essential, since the progress of the disease is rapid under favourable conditions for mushroom culture.
